newsitem.title: UK: Aboriginal tells Britain to return ancestor's head.
newsitem.headline: Aboriginal tells Britain to return ancestor's head.

text.p: An Aboriginal leader arrived in Britain on Tuesday and vowed he would not return to Western Australia without the severed head of a famous ancestor buried in an English cemetery.

Ken Colbung and native Australians have been haggling with the British government since the head of Yagan, an Aboriginal leader in the 1820s in the Swan River district near Perth, was traced to its current resting place in Liverpool, northern England, in 1993.
But they have been thwarted by British government red tape and complicated exhumation procedures.
"We want that head back when I leave the shores of England next week," Colbung told a news conference.
"Yagan must return to Australia with me and I'm not going to leave without it. It's very important to us. It's a spiritual obligation."

The bearded 66-year-old who has the backing of the Australian government, said he wanted a meeting with Home Secretary (interior minister) Jack Straw to plead his case and would do whatever it took to get the head back.

Colbung accused Britain of stealing the head after Yagan was killed in 1833. It was sent to Britain where it was displayed in the Liverpool Royal Institution and then in the city museum before being buried.

Britain refused Colbung's application to have the head exhumed because the bodies of 20 stillborn babies were interred in a mass burial above Yagan's remains and could not be disturbed without the parents' permission.

"I see it as perhaps some form of racial bias against us, the Aboriginal people, that the British government is using the mothers of these babies as pawns in an argument not to return something that belongs to us. Something that they stole from us 168 years ago and are not prepared to give up."

Colbung said Britain did not understand the importance of the skull to Aboriginals who believe that Yagan cannot enter the spirit world and be reincarnated because his head is separated from his torso.
He said that, in the days of his ancestors, the matter would have been settled between him and Straw in a spear fight, but he hoped his diplomatic efforts would succeed.
"We sincerely hope the pen can be mightier than the sword," he added. "Mr Jack Straw should open the door."

In addition to pushing for a meeting with Straw, Colbung plans to publish an open letter to the parents of the children asking for their permission to disturb the graves. Only five parents from the 20 are contactable and two have already given their consent.
"I would certainly hope they can support me in this effort to get the head back," Colbung said.
